title: One by one
hookLine: Sariputta knew each state one by one as it arose
carry: each piece is small and passing

cards: A sommelier tastes a wine and says: cherry, then leather, then something like pencil shavings. You taste the same glass and get: red. Same sip.

The difference is training: noticing things one at a time, in the order they come. The hundred and eleventh discourse opens with the Buddha praising his student Sariputta, and the praise is very specific.
For half a month, the Buddha says, Sariputta saw his own mind's states one by one, as they came.

teach.h: ANUPADA: ONE BY ONE, IN ORDER
teach.b: The discourse is called Anupada: one by one, in succession, step after step. The Buddha calls Sariputta wise, with great wisdom, wide, quick and penetrating, then shows what that looked like.
Sariputta enters the first meditative absorption, and inside it he doesn't just feel calm. He picks out what's there: applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, ease, a mind gathered to one point.
Contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind. Zeal, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, attention. A long list, and he knows each one.

The key line, paraphrased: each was known as it arose, known as it stayed, known as it passed. They hadn't been, and came to be; having been, they vanished. So he wasn't attracted to them or repelled by them.

teach.h: A TRUE SON, ROLLING THE WHEEL
teach.b: He goes on through the deeper absorptions and the formless attainments. At the subtlest ones, where states can't be picked out as they happen, he looks back on them after he comes out.
Why does this matter for someone who isn't a monk in deep absorption? An inner life can feel like one big weather system: I'm stressed, I'm fine.
A meditator learns to see the parts: a tight jaw, a worried thought, a flicker of hope, a sound. Seen one at a time, each piece is small and passing.
The Buddha ends by calling Sariputta his true son, born of the teaching, who keeps rolling the wheel the Buddha set turning.

how: In insight meditation as taught in many Theravada centers, practitioners make light mental notes of what arises (hearing, thinking, feeling) one moment at a time, a method that draws on discourses like MN 111 and the foundations of mindfulness.

o: over and over, the same thing again
one by one, each thing in its turn
all at once, in a single flash

games.q: one by one: tap the pairs.
p: how long Sariputta practiced this way
born of the teaching, rolling the wheel

s: in MN 111 Sariputta just felt calm and didn't examine it
he picked out each state in the absorption: thought, rapture, feeling, intention, mindfulness and more.
the Buddha praises Sariputta for seeing states arise and pass
not having been, they came to be; having been, they vanished.
the discourse is named for a place
anupada means one by one, in succession: it names the method.

games.q: you're in deep calm, and pleasant states fill the mind. what did Sariputta do, according to MN 111?
o: hold on to them as long as possible.
know each one arising, staying and passing.
games.why: he knew each one in turn, saw it come and go, and so was neither attracted nor repelled.

practice: When something shows up, give it one soft word: hearing, itching, planning, calm, doubt. Don't hunt for things or fix them; just name what comes, in the order it comes, and notice that each one, after a while, isn't there anymore.

wordCard.voice: Anupada. The discourse where Sariputta is praised for seeing each state of his mind arise, stay and pass, one by one, step by step.

orig.note: Pali anupada: step by step, one after another. the title of MN 111.

carryVoice: Your line: each piece is small and passing. Even a storm of a mood is made of parts. Day four eighty-four, done.
